# What alignment adds

Alignment optimization estimates approximate parameter comparability without
imposing exact equality on every loading and intercept. It is often most useful
with many groups, where long exact-invariance sequences become impractical. It
does not prove invariance or automatically justify latent-mean comparisons.

`inv_align_auto()` accepts item-level data or group-by-item loading and
intercept matrices. Matrix inputs must contain parameters from compatible
configural measurement models; observed item means are not substitutes for
factor intercepts.

# Compact matrix workflow

The matrices below are illustrative configural-model parameters with explicit
group and item identities.

```{r matrices}
groups <- c("A", "B")
items <- paste0("i", 1:9)

lambda <- rbind(
  A = c(0.78, 0.73, 0.76, 0.72, 0.80, 0.69, 0.77, 0.74, 0.71),
  B = c(0.76, 0.75, 0.72, 0.74, 0.78, 0.71, 0.75, 0.76, 0.70)
)
nu <- rbind(
  A = rep(0, length(items)),
  B = c(0.03, -0.02, 0.45, 0.01, -0.03, 0.02, 0.00, 0.02, -0.01)
)
dimnames(lambda) <- dimnames(nu) <- list(groups, items)
```

```{r alignment, eval = FALSE}
if (requireNamespace("sirt", quietly = TRUE)) {
  alignment <- PsychoMatic::inv_align_auto(
    lambda = lambda,
    nu = nu,
    fixed = TRUE,
    meth = 2,
    language = "eng"
  )
  summary(alignment)
}
```

The alignment chunk is not evaluated during vignette construction because the
optional optimization engine can be slow on constrained workers. The installed
example executes the same bounded workflow.

# Interpretation and diagnostics

Named matrices and weights are matched by group/item identity. Missing,
ambiguous, or duplicate identities are rejected rather than paired by accident.
Engine errors, nonconvergence, malformed dimensions, and non-finite objectives
produce a structured `not_evaluable` result without favorable prose.

Alignment R-squared and the percentage of non-invariant parameters are
approximate diagnostics that depend on tuning, tolerance, model quality, and
the number/diversity of groups. A cutoff is a heuristic rather than a formal
test. Inspect item/group flags, the objective and convergence evidence,
requested/effective settings, missingness diagnostics, and sensitivity to
reasonable tuning values. With only two groups, conventional complete or
researcher-directed partial invariance will often be easier to interpret.

Use `factorial_invariance_auto()` for a complete exact-invariance sequence and
`invariance_partial()` for explicitly justified releases with anchors.
`psychomatic_report()` can then export the structured evidence from whichever
workflow matches the research question.
